subject: D49918E5C4014E13A7AD43BCB1E89561
introduction: To be known completely is either a terror or a comfort, and scripture has spoken of it as both. These few readings begin with the comfort: not a leaf stirs but God knows it, and the secrets of hearts are “openly manifest in the holy Presence.” They then take up the question that has followed the doctrine in every religion: if God knows what I will do, am I free? ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s answer, like the Báb’s and Bahá’u’lláh’s, is that knowledge of a thing is not its cause; a gardener who knows which fruit will be bitter did not make it so. One reading turns to conduct: God’s forbearance is mistaken for ignorance. Psalm 139, the sparrow of the Gospel and the Qur’án’s “nearer than his jugular vein” stand with the first theme. Milton gives the same answer about foreknowledge almost in the same words; Ben Sira states human freedom bluntly; and FitzGerald’s Omar Khayyám speaks for those who feel carried along “willy-nilly.”
questions: “Think not the secrets of hearts are hidden.” Do you hear this first as warning or as comfort, and what does your answer tell you?
“The knowledge of a thing is not the cause of its occurrence.” Test the gardener’s example: where does it persuade you, and where do you still feel the difficulty?
God’s forbearance “hath emboldened souls.” Ecclesiastes says the same. How should patience that is mistaken for absence be understood by the one who benefits from it?
Paul hopes to know “even as also I am known.” How might being known by God change the way you try to know yourself?

outside.why: A gardener knows which fruit will be bitter and which sweet, “but this knowledge does not cause it to happen.” Milton has God say the same of the angels who fell: if I foreknew, foreknowledge had no influence on their fault.
Knowledge of a thing before it appears. The word that came to Jeremiah: before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee.
“Not a leaf stirreth except that God knoweth its movement.” The sentence echoes the Qur’án: not a leaf falleth but He knoweth it, not a grain amid the darkness of the earth.
Jesus draws comfort from the same thought: one sparrow shall not fall on the ground without your Father; the very hairs of your head are all numbered.
“Think not the secrets of hearts are hidden.” Psalm 139: thou understandest my thought afar off; there is not a word in my tongue, but, lo, O Lord, thou knowest it altogether.
Hebrews: all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do.
His knowledge of all things before they exist is like His knowledge after. Isaiah: declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done.
God’s knowledge “encompasses the realities of all things.” The Throne Verse: He knoweth all that is before them and all that is behind them, while they cannot compass it in knowledge.

Foreknown, and still free. Ben Sira states the freedom without qualification: He left him in the hand of his counsel; stretch forth thy hand unto whether thou wilt. How do the readings keep both sentences true?

FitzGerald’s Omar concludes from a world already known that nothing is ours to decide: into this Universe, and why not knowing, nor whence, like Water willy-nilly flowing. What in the gardener’s example answers him?
The Qur’án rests God’s knowledge on His making: should He not know what He created?
On the name “All-Seeing.” The psalmist’s argument: he that planted the ear, shall he not hear? he that formed the eye, shall he not see?
“He knoweth your deeds before their appearance.” The Qur’án: We know what his soul whispereth to him, and We are nearer to him than his jugular vein.

“The forbearance of God hath emboldened souls … most people imagine that God is unaware.” Ecclesiastes observed it: because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil.
Peter gives the reason for the delay: the Lord is not slack, but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish.

“All knowledge is divine knowledge.” Paul looks forward to a knowing that answers to being known: then shall I know even as also I am known. What difference does it make to live as one already fully known?

psalm-thou-hast-searched-me.text: O lord, thou hast searched me, and known me. Thou knowest my downsitting and mine uprising, thou understandest my thought afar off. Thou compassest my path and my lying down, and art acquainted with all my ways. For there is not a word in my tongue, but, lo, O Lord, thou knowest it altogether

hebrews-naked-and-opened.text: Neither is there any creature that is not manifest in his sight: but all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do

psalm-he-that-formed-the-eye.text: Yet they say, The Lord shall not see, neither shall the God of Jacob regard it. Understand, ye brutish among the people: and ye fools, when will ye be wise? He that planted the ear, shall he not hear? he that formed the eye, shall he not see

proverbs-eyes-of-the-lord-in-every-place.text: The eyes of the Lord are in every place, beholding the evil and the good

quran-should-he-not-know-what-he-created.text: Should He not know what He created? And He is the Subtile, the Aware.
